Laboratory cultures of the amphipod Monocorophium insidiosum maintained at 10 °C [T = 10 °C] reveal a developmental trajectory strongly modulated by temperature. Newly hatched juveniles emerged from the maternal brood pouch at a total length of 0.15 cm [Lb = 0.15 cm], a measurement consistent across repeated observations. The embryonic period, defined as the interval from ovum deposition to the onset of exogenous feeding, lasted approximately 10.0 days [ab = approximately 10.0 days], after which the free-swimming larvae began filter feeding on suspen at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]ded microalgae. This relatively protracted incubation phase is typical for corophiid amphipods experiencing cool thermal regimes, where metabolic rates are depressed and developmental processes slow accordingly. Following the larval-juvenile transition, the growing juveniles entered a period of rapid somatic growth punctuated by successive moulting events. The age at which individuals attained sexual maturation was considerably delayed under these conditions, with puberty occurring at 99.0 days after birth [tp = 99.0 days after birth] at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. Furthermore, the total duration of life was extended, as the maximum lifespan recorded under constant 10 °C conditions reached 223.0 days [am = 223.0 days], reflecting the inverse relationship between temperature and longevity commonly observed in small benthic crustaceans at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C].

When rearing temperature was elevated to 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the pace of life history events accelerated markedly for Monocorophium insidiosum. The age at birth, measured from egg fertilisation to the emergence of the first active feeding juvenile, declined to 5.0 days [ab = 5.0 days], representing a substantial reduction compared to cooler conditions at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. Correspondingly, the time required to reach reproductive maturity contracted, as individuals attained puberty at 52.0 days following birth [tp = 52.0 days following birth], a value that highlights the thermal sensitivity of gonadal development in this species at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. Adult females under this regime also demonstrated a notable lifetime fecundity, producing an average of 88.0 offspring  over the course of their reproductive lifespan at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This elevated output likely reflects a combination of faster brood cycling and extended breeding duration relative to the colder treatment. Maximum longevity at 15 °C was recorded at 152.0 days [am = 152.0 days], a reduction from the 10 °C cohort that aligns with the general principle of increased metabolic expenditure and accelerated senescence at higher temperatures at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. The trade-off between rapid maturation and shortened lifespan is a recurring theme in the thermal biology of small-bodied peracarids.

Further warming to 20 °C [T = 20 °C] compressed the developmental schedule of Monocorophium insidiosum even more dramatically. The embryonic stage was completed in just 4.0 days [ab = 4.0 days], among the shortest incubation periods documented for this species under controlled laboratory settings at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Sexual maturation followed swiftly, with puberty recorded at 29.0 days after birth [tp = 29.0 days after birth], a value that underscores the powerful influence of elevated temperature on the acceleration of gametogenesis and the onset of brood production at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Despite this rapid early development, overall lifetime offspring production at 20 °C averaged 83.0 offspring , slightly lower than the peak observed at 15 °C, suggesting that while warmer conditions hasten maturation, they may impose physiological costs that curtail total reproductive output at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Adult lifespan at this thermal extreme was 142.0 days [am = 142.0 days], the shortest of the three temperature treatments examined at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. The energetic demands of maintaining a high metabolic rate in warm water, coupled with the accelerated pace of reproduction, likely contribute to the earlier onset of physiological senescence and mortality in this cohort.

Sexual dimorphism in body size is a prominent feature of Monocorophium insidiosum, with adult females attaining a greater ultimate body length than their male counterparts. Gravid, ovigerous females measured in laboratory populations reached a maximum adult length of 0.56 cm [Li = 0.56 cm], a size that facilitates the accommodation of a substantial brood within the marsupium. In contrast, sexually mature males were consistently smaller, achieving an ultimate body length of 0.42 cm [Li = 0.42 cm], a difference that likely reflects divergent selective pressures on male versus female growth trajectories. The body length at which individuals first became reproductively active, measured at the onset of puberty, was 0.41 cm [Lp = 0.41 cm], indicating that both sexes begin gametogenesis at a comparable somatic size threshold. The ultimate dry weight of fully grown, reproductively mature adults was determined to be 0.000502 grams , a modest biomass that aligns with the small body size typical of tube-dwelling amphipods inhabiting estuarine soft sediments. This low individual mass likely influences the species' energy allocation strategies and its role as a prey item for juvenile fish and larger invertebrates.

The reproductive ecology of Monocorophium insidiosum is characterized by iteroparous breeding, with females producing multiple broods over their relatively compressed lifespans. Field-collected adults brought into the laboratory and maintained at 10 °C [T = 10 °C] produced an average of only 46.0 offspring  across their entire reproductive tenure, the lowest lifetime fecundity recorded among the three experimental temperatures. This reduced output at cooler conditions is consistent with the slower brood development and longer inter-brood intervals that accompany depressed metabolic rates. At 15 °C [T = 15 °C], lifetime fecundity peaked at 88.0 offspring , representing a thermal optimum for reproductive performance in this population. The slight decline to 83.0 offspring  at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] suggests that while warm temperatures accelerate brood cycling, they may also impose a physiological ceiling on total output, possibly due to increased maintenance costs or reduced allocation of resources to each successive clutch. Overall, the species demonstrates a clear capacity for thermal adaptation, with temperature serving as a primary driver of both the timing and magnitude of reproductive investment throughout the adult stage.
